verdict: Caution: lend to downstream service and logistics SMEs tied to the Bathinda refinery, not to refining or coal-product units themselves; the data call is Caution and the news flow is worse, so no upgrade.
title: Bathinda Petroleum Refining & Coal Products: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Refining is a spread business, not a demand business: crude goes in, products come out, and cash is made on the gap between the two, not on volume.** The Bathinda complex is the anchor here, and the local coverage we hold is thin — sources [1], [2] and [3] are topic pages with no usable figures, so treat this note as first principles plus peer evidence. **The value sits in the crude-to-product spread and in inventory timing, and both move against a small borrower fast.** Crude is bought in dollars at landed cost; product prices are set by the market and, for the retail side, by administered pricing. So when a proposal lands, check the borrower's actual role — trader, transporter, service contractor, or converter — before you discuss any limit.

## Where cash sits and what has changed
**Working capital is the whole game: crude and product inventory plus receivables from oil marketing companies, and the receivable clock is set by the buyer, not the borrower.** Peer results show the spread swinging hard: HPCL's GRM rose to US$32.2/bbl, up 35% QoQ and 262% YoY, on throughput of 6.2mmt, down 5% QoQ and 6% YoY [7]; BPCL's quarter turned on Brent at around $70 per barrel from mid-July [4]; IOC reported domestic under-recovery of INR 184 per cylinder in September, INR 229 in October, projected at INR 309 in November and INR 370 in December [6]. **Margin is being made on price, not on volume, and that is exactly the kind of profit that reverses.** Nationally, IIP NIC 19 output is -0.6% YoY and -0.9% Apr-to-date [D], so the physical volume base is shrinking even as spreads widen. Punjab GST collections are +9.7% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D] — a real local tailwind, but it is a consumption signal, not a refining signal.

## Who to pursue now, and who to avoid
**Pursue the downstream service layer: tanker and bulk logistics operators, tank-farm and turnaround contractors, testing and inspection firms, and packaging and lubricant-blending units with diversified customers.** These earn fees, not spreads, and their cash cycle is short. **Avoid standalone refining and coal-product converters, and any borrower whose order book is one refinery or one oil marketing company.** Rating commentary is explicit that nominee-clearing ability drives liquidity in this chain [10], and ICRA's HMEL view rests on HPCL sponsor support, not on standalone strength [8]. If a proposal is a single-buyer converter, ask for the buyer's payment history and the contract term before anything else.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the receivable, not the refinery's balance sheet: invoice discounting or a receivables line with the oil marketing company as the acknowledged payer, and keep tenor inside the payment cycle.** Take monthly: GST returns, e-way bills, the receivable ageing by buyer, and bank statements showing actual collections. **Set a covenant that concentration with any single buyer stays below a stated share, and price for the spread cycle rather than the last quarter's margin.** Where a figure is missing — throughput, contract value, buyer payment days — write 'collect from customer' and do not fill the gap with an estimate.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for margin-led profit that does not repeat: if a borrower's best quarter coincides with a GRM spike like the one in [7], ask what the next two quarters look like at a normal spread.** A drop in throughput with rising margin is a warning, not a comfort. **If receivables from the oil marketing company stretch beyond the contract term, cut the limit before the next drawdown.** Note that the rating sources [8], [9], [10] and [11] are undated or old — [11] is from 2017 — so do not lean on them for current numbers.
